title: What was the Skeleton Army?
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck open with tour dates for the Pacific Northwest swing and a welcome to new puppy Gibson, then explore the Skeleton Army, the anti-Salvation Army street movement in 1870s–1880s England. They cover the Salvation Army's founding by George Booth and his wife Catherine Mumford, its street preaching, pub incursions, and militaristic style; the violent backlash (riots, dead rats, urine attacks, the death of Captain Susannah Beattie); the likely roots in Bonfire Clubs and Guy Fawkes Night; the Riot Act; the court case Beatty v. Gillbanks on peaceable assembly; and the Skokie Nazi march case. The episode closes with a listener mail item from John about sailors who could not swim, and a sign-off.

segments.title: Opening banter and new puppy
segments.summary: Hosts banter, credit listener Corey Wegner for the topic, and welcome new foster puppy Gibson, a coonhound-shepherd mix, to the family.

segments.title: Is the Salvation Army a fake army?
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh debate what counts as an army, then introduce the Salvation Army and its mission to combat poverty, founded in the late 1870s and noted for its Christian roots and controversial views on LGBTQ people.

segments.title: George Booth and the founding
segments.summary: George Booth, a Methodist preacher born in Nottingham in 1829, became frustrated with church hierarchy and started street preaching. His wife Catherine Mumford also preached, which was progressive for the time.

segments.title: Army forward origins, mottos and music
segments.summary: In 1878 Booth renamed his Christian Mission the Salvation Army, and the group adopted military ranks, uniforms, and terms like War Cry. Their motto was soup, soap, salvation, and they were strongly anti-alcohol. They used loud music and drums, and the hosts digress into Stryper.

segments.title: Salvation Army tactics that angered pub-goers
segments.summary: The Salvation Army went into pubs and streets singing hymns and banging drums to reach sinners. Pub-goers and others resented the intrusions, and the group's hostile, assertive style made it a nuisance.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode ad break before the Skeleton Army origin discussion.

segments.title: Origins of the Skeleton Army counter-movement
segments.summary: The Skeleton Army formed as a counter-movement to the Salvation Army, starting with jeering and escalating into violence. The first recorded clash was in Liverpool in 1879, followed by an 1881 attack in London's East End on Salvationist women.

segments.title: Violence against Salvationists and parody songs
segments.summary: Violence included ropes, hot coals, dead rats and cats, urine, and a meeting disrupted by chamber pot attackers. Statistics cited: 669 Salvationists assaulted, 56 buildings attacked, 86 imprisoned. The Salvation Army parodied pub songs with Christian lyrics, such as 'The Devil in Me'.

segments.title: Salvationist counter-tactics and pub culture
segments.summary: The Salvation Army sang 'Out of the Gutters We Pick Them' and grew despite opposition. The Skeleton Army retaliated by tarring alleys and throwing blue-paint eggs, and the mottoes were mocked. The hosts reflect on rowdy pub patrons.

segments.title: Death of Susannah Beattie
segments.summary: Captain Susannah Beattie died in 1881 or 1882 after she was beaten by the Skeleton Army. The Salvation Army names her its first martyr. A Skeleton Army member was also killed by a police baton.

segments.title: Authorities, brewers, and why the hostility spread
segments.summary: Police and courts were largely hostile to the Salvation Army, and local power structures opposed it. Brewers and their employees fought back against temperance. Protestant and Catholic groups also opposed the Salvation Army. Ada Smith and Worthing riots are discussed, with town type affecting violence.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode ad break before the discussion of Skeleton Army origins.

segments.title: Bonfire Clubs and Guy Fawkes Night roots
segments.summary: Historian John Hare argued the Skeleton Armies grew out of Bonfire Clubs that celebrated the fifth of November. A 1885 Sussex Coast Mercury article described a Skeleton Club in Worthing using an old Bonfire Club banner. The Gunpowder Plot of 1605 is explained as the origin of Guy Fawkes Night.

segments.title: Skeleton Army disguises and the Riot Act
segments.summary: Skeleton Army members blackened their faces, wore masks, and identified each other with yellow ribbons or sunflowers. The 1714 British Riot Act is explained, which ordered rioters to disperse, and authorities called out troops when rioting continued.

segments.title: Tangent on Stryper and D Snyder
segments.summary: The hosts joke about Stryper and their album titles, and recall meeting D Snyder at a talk show.

segments.title: Peaceable assembly and Beatty v. Gillbanks
segments.summary: The Salvation Army was held responsible in court for riots its presence provoked. An appellate court later ruled in Beatty v. Gillbanks (1882) that a lawful assembly is not criminal merely because it may provoke unlawful acts by others. The hosts then discuss the 1977 National Socialist Party of America v. Village of Skokie case on free speech.

segments.title: Listener mail: non-swimming sailors
segments.summary: Listener John writes about a Franklin Expedition episode pun and shares a nugget from Peter Stark's book Astoria on why many sailors could not swim, linked to the Astor fur trade colony at Astoria, Oregon.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank John for the listener mail, invite more suggestions, and sign off.
